# Purpose of This Document

This is a management summary, not a specification. It reports whether the S1
testing-mode implementation actually behaves as `technology/consensus-transition.md`
and `analysis/Rincoin_840k_S1_Consensus_Change_Specification.qmd` say it should
— checked by running it, not by re-reading the design. Derivations and the
normative rule itself live in those documents; this one only reports what was
run, against what, and what happened. The full evidence — every test case, raw
logs, exact commits — is in [`S1/`](S1/), not repeated here.

Two things this document is trying to establish, and only these two:

1. **The implementation withstands real conditions**, not just its own test
   suite in isolation — including other, differently-behaving node software it
   actually meets on a shared network.
2. **A technically skilled reader can verify the first claim without reading
   the design documents, the source code, or the CI logs themselves** — this
   document plus its annex is sufficient on its own.

The rest of the document is in three parts: **Summary** gives the outcome in a
few lines; **Methods** describes what was tested and how, grouped the same way
throughout; **Results** reports, group by group, whether it passed.

# What Changes at H1, Briefly

At block height 840,000 (mainnet), three things change together: the block
subsidy schedule (recursive floor(previous × 19/20) per 210,000-block epoch,
no floor, no tail), a scheduled coinbase commitment identifying the chosen
schedule, and a sighash-level replay identifier (`sig_fork_id`) mixed into
new transaction signatures. Full rationale and byte-level specification:
`technology/consensus-transition.md`. This document assumes that design and
tests it; it does not re-argue it.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.95\textwidth]{figures/s1_subsidy_curve.png}
\caption{Maximum permitted block subsidy under the S1 candidate, independently
re-derived from the published recursive rule (not imported from the
implementation under test) and confirmed to agree with all 34 applicable rows
of \texttt{analysis/data/S1\_normative\_test\_vectors.csv}, the specification's
own conformance vector file.}
\end{figure}
```

# Summary

**Every test that has been run passes.** 532 of 532 C++ unit tests, 159 of 159
functional tests (the fork-specific suite plus the full pre-existing CI
allowlist, unmodified), and every cross-implementation comparison run so far.
Two real defects were found and fixed while building this evidence, reported
in Results as part of it, not as a caveat against it.

{{< include includes/s1_results_summary_table.qmd >}}

One evidence layer is not yet complete: the full cross-implementation
producer × validator matrix (comparing this implementation against older
Rincoin releases and independently developed forks, in both directions, run
by a reusable tool rather than the two narrower hand-written comparisons
currently in place). Two related, narrower comparisons that *are* done are
reported in Results §5.4, including a real finding about a currently-released
Rincoin version's actual behavior at the fork height.

Read **Methods** below for what "tested" means in each row above and why it
was tested that way; read **Results** for the detail behind each pass.

# Methods: What Was Tested, and How

Four groups, used consistently through both this section and Results:

| Group | What it checks | Why it's a separate group |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit-level | Each piece of consensus logic (subsidy formula, commitment parsing, sighash mixing) against frozen, byte-exact vectors | Smallest testable unit; catches an error before it can reach anything that depends on it |
| Single-node functional | The same rules, enforced end-to-end by a real running node via RPC/P2P | Unit tests exercise logic in-process; this confirms the rules hold when driven the way a real deployment would drive them |
| Multi-node functional | Whether the network prefers higher work only when that chain is also rule-valid | This is the entire reason the coinbase-commitment mechanism exists — it has to be checked directly, not inferred from the rule existing |
| Cross-implementation | What happens when this build meets software that disagrees with it | The only layer that reflects the network as it actually is, not just this codebase |

## Unit-level

The subsidy formula, the coinbase-commitment builder/parser, and the
`sig_fork_id` sighash-mixing code are each checked in isolation against
frozen vectors — values fixed in advance, not computed by calling the code
under test. For the subsidy formula specifically, "frozen" means two
independent sources agreeing: `analysis/data/S1_normative_test_vectors.csv`
(the file the specification itself names as the conformance target) and a
from-scratch Python re-derivation of the published recursive rule
(`verification/scripts/independently_derive_s1_schedule.py`) that does not
import the C++ implementation, mirroring
`analysis/scripts/verify_s6b_independently.py`'s existing role for S6/b.

Every pre-existing sighash and script unit test in the codebase is also
re-run, unmodified, as a no-regression guard — confirming the new sighash
mixing produces byte-identical output for every caller that doesn't opt into
it.

## Single-node functional

Driven through a real, running `rincoind` process via its actual RPC and P2P
interfaces (the same `TestNode` framework `analysis/`'s own reproducibility
scripts assume readers are comfortable with), not exercised in-process:
coinbase-commitment validation (every malformation in the vector catalog, see
[`S1/commitment-test-vectors.md`](S1/commitment-test-vectors.md)), subsidy
enforcement at and around the activation boundary, and `sig_fork_id`
transaction propagation and rejection before and after activation.

## Multi-node functional

Two testing-mode nodes, connected and synced past the activation height, one
isolated and used to mine two competing continuations: a longer chain that is
also commitment-valid, and a longer chain that is commitment-*invalid*. Both
chains are offered back to the network; which one is adopted is the entire
test.

## Cross-implementation

Every accessible node binary — this implementation, older Rincoin releases,
and independently developed forks reachable on a shared network — tested as
both block *producer* and block *validator* against every other binary, with
expected outcomes taken from the frozen vectors above, never from any
implementation's own output (so no single binary is treated as ground truth).

::: {.callout-note}
## Editorial note — for maintainers

The general-purpose tool that runs this comparison for an arbitrary set of
binaries (`test/fork_interop_matrix.py`, so the same tool serves S5/b and
S6/b later without being rewritten) is not yet built. Two narrower,
hand-written comparisons currently stand in for it —
`feature_fork_vs_legacy.py` and `feature_fork_vs_aevust.py` — and their
results are reported in Results §5.4.
:::

# Results: Did It Pass?

Same four groups as Methods, each reporting a concrete outcome, not a
restated description of the test.

## Unit-level — pass

532 of 532 C++ unit tests pass. (One unrelated, pre-existing warning: a
missing test-data environment variable skips a single unit test; not a
failure, not introduced by this work.)

The subsidy schedule's two independent sources — the specification's own
normative vector file and the from-scratch Python re-derivation — agree with
each other and with the C++ implementation at every height checked:

{{< include includes/s1_vector_spotcheck_table.qmd >}}

The commitment-parsing vector catalog is covered with two specific
exceptions, tracked individually rather than folded into a round number: see
[`S1/commitment-test-vectors.md`](S1/commitment-test-vectors.md) for exactly
which two and why.

This is also the layer where both real defects mentioned in the Summary were
actually found — both by unit tests written for this work, not by code
review:

- A wallet operation crashed the whole test process (not just failed the one
  operation) when exercised on a wallet that hadn't yet processed a block,
  via an overly strict internal assertion newly reached by this branch's
  fork-context lookup. First visible as 91 unrelated-looking failures in a
  completely different part of the test suite; traced with a debugger to this
  root cause.
- The component that produces `sig_fork_id`-aware signatures had a latent bug
  that made its own internal self-check reject its own correctly created
  signatures — a real defect on the PSBT-signing path (confirmed against the
  actual call sites, not a test-only artifact), caught by a unit test written
  specifically to exercise that path directly rather than through a wrapper
  that happened to route around the bug.

Full detail and reproduction commands: [`S1/unit-test-results.md`](S1/unit-test-results.md).

## Single-node functional — pass

All commitment-validation, subsidy-enforcement, and `sig_fork_id` checks pass
against a real running node, across every boundary and malformation case
tested. Part of a 159-test functional run that also re-runs every
pre-existing (non-fork-specific) functional test unmodified, confirming no
regression to ordinary wallet, mempool, P2P, mining, or MWEB behavior.

## Multi-node functional — pass

Both reorg outcomes are correct: the higher-work, commitment-*valid* chain is
adopted; the higher-work, commitment-*invalid* chain is not — confirming the
mechanism does what it exists to do, not just that a valid chain is accepted.

`-reindex-chainstate` was additionally checked empirically across the
activation height (mine past H1, restart with `-reindex-chainstate`, compare
tip and `verifychain`): identical tip, clean result. This does not by itself
re-run block-acceptance-time consensus checks — a pre-existing, long-standing
property shared by every other height-gated consensus rule already in this
codebase, not something specific to this branch — so it's reported as a
confirmation that behavior matches that established property, not as an
independent re-validation.

## Cross-implementation — partially done, passing so far

The full producer × validator matrix has not been run (see the Methods
editorial note). Two narrower comparisons have, and both pass for what they
cover:

- **S1 vs. `v1.1.0`** (`rincoin-community/rincoin-core`): clean divergence at
  the activation height — this implementation applies its rules, `v1.1.0`
  does not adopt it. A genuine finding surfaced along the way: `v1.1.0`
  itself does **not** halt or refuse to extend the chain past height 840,000
  on a non-mainnet chain, contradicting that release's own stated branch
  policy (whose halt height turned out to be wired for mainnet only).
  Reported as a finding about that release's actual, directly observed
  behavior, not about S1.
- **S1 vs. `v1.0.1`** (`Rin-coin/rincoin`, no fork awareness at all): clean
  divergence, no crash, no accidental adoption of the S1 chain — confirmed
  directly via `getbestblockhash` on both nodes.
- **S1 vs. `Aevust/rincoin@feature/port-sim-v1.0.7`** (an independently
  developed, foreign fork): the foreign branch's headers can become this
  node's best-known-header, but full-block validation correctly rejects it at
  H1 for a missing/wrong commitment — the validated tip
  (`getbestblockhash`) never adopts it, even while header-tracking RPCs see
  it.

Full detail: [`S1/functional-test-results.md`](S1/functional-test-results.md).

# Scope: What This Testing Does Not Cover

Deliberate scoping, not oversight:

- **Header-level branch isolation** (a block-header version bit as a second,
  independent identity mechanism) — designed and then dropped from the
  active proposal; kept only as a fully specified, inactive contingency. Not
  part of what S1 actually implements, so not tested.
- **A dedicated P2P branch-announcement message** — no such message exists in
  the current design (commitment-only + `sig_fork_id`); an earlier,
  since-abandoned draft used one.
- **Staged release engineering** (build profiles, signalling windows,
  cross-party coordination gates) — production-deployment planning for
  *after* a scenario is selected. Nothing is selected yet. This
  implementation is a single testing-mode build that refuses to run on
  mainnet at all without an explicit environment variable set at every
  invocation; that is the right level of complexity for what it currently is.
- **Live mainnet telemetry or monitoring** — not applicable; this build
  cannot run on mainnet.
- **Pool- and DNS-seeder-software integration rehearsals** — real-world
  integration points worth covering (a pool rebuilding the coinbase
  transaction is exactly the kind of place a commitment silently gets
  stripped), tracked as outstanding rather than silently skipped:
  [`S1/open-items.md`](S1/open-items.md).
